items.title: Welcome to the Scrolling Backlash
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube A lot of people are getting tired of their phone—they’re sick of the algorithms and overwhelmed by what can feel like a loss of control. The Atlantic staff writer Julie Beck dug into why and how people are trying to renegotiate their relationships with technology. She and our colleagues just released a five-part podcast series called How to Touch Grass , and in this episode, Galaxy Brain host Charlie Warzel talks with Beck about why people are nostalgic for the pre-internet days, how our brains are changing, and the good that can come from getting lost. The following is a transcript of the episode: Charlie Warzel: How does the phone make you feel? How does a TikTok binge make you feel, or even just, like, a before-bed scrolling session that we all have? Julie Beck: Oh, sick. Absolutely sick. It’s like when the aliens get you, right? They take you up and then they probe you, or they do whatever they do, and then when you come back down, you don’t know what happened. It’s erased. It’s lost time. So I feel like I have emerged from lost time and like what happened during that time is unclear, but I don’t feel good. Warzel: I don’t know that I have the amnesia part of it, but it promotes self-loathing in a way that like truly no other activity does because it just feels like a deletion of my one precious life. I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain , a show where today we’re gonna answer a question. Maybe it’s even the question of the online age. How can we live lives where we use tech and don’t let it use us? This is the animating question of How to Touch Grass , a new podcast series by my colleagues here at The Atlantic . Over five episodes, Julie Beck and her co-host and producer, Natalie Brennan, explore what exactly is happening in this moment that has so many of us out there feeling like we need to renegotiate our relationships to our technology. At the beginning of this year, I made a few predictions about trends that we might see, and one of them was that there would be what I was calling a scrolling backlash. That people are just really tired of their phones, of the algorithmic internet, of this idea that they’re being manipulated all the time, and that their attention is being directed towards things that don’t make them feel good or whole or happy. Now, as predictions go, this is a pretty safe one, but it’s really been borne out in recent months. These things are hard to measure, but you can just feel it out there in the world. In the artists who are asking that people leave their phones at home or in their pockets at concerts, in the genuine concern over whether younger generations are going to be able to read like older generations. And while the data-center backlash that we’re seeing right now is complicated, and it’s about a lot of things, including AI, I also see that as an outgrowth of this larger frustration about the role that big tech is playing in our lives and the way that people just feel this fuzzy loss of agency right now. It’s a loss that just can’t be separated from the devices that we use. How to Touch Grass digs into so many of the ideas that I’ve been trying to poke at here in the first year of this podcast. Our motto here at Galaxy Brain is that we pay attention to where we pay attention, which also happens to be exactly what I found so valuable about Julie and Natalie’s work. And so I decided to bring Julie on here today to talk about this moment and to talk about what she’s learned in this series. How badly have our attention spans actually been fractured? How has she reevaluated her relationship to all of her devices? Is the backlash that we’re feeling and seeing right now justified? And crucially, where might we go from here? Julie joins me now to talk about it all. [ Music ] Warzel: Julie, welcome to Galaxy Brain . Julie Beck: Hi, Charlie. Thanks for having me. Warzel: So let’s talk about this. Let’s talk about the touch-grass moment that I think we are in. Even even the phrase itself, right? Why is “touching grass” something that people are talking about? And what made you want to just dig in and report on it? Beck: Yes. So we had originally thought about calling the season How to Log Off , but that’s not as fun. But I think it also speaks to just a sort of general renegotiation that people are doing right now between how much they actually want to be on their devices and how much they actually want to be inhabiting the embodied world around you and the grass and the trees and the people and everybody around you. We wanted to look at like the various shifts that are happening both in the culture of the internet itself and the technology itself but also the shifts in the culture of how people are thinking about their devices and how they’re talking about them, and how much they want to use them. Warzel: Why did you feel like this was a project you wanted to embark on? Beck: I have deleted and re-downloaded TikTok on my phone roughly four to five times. Warzel: Nice. Beck: And it’s usually like my friend ends up sending me a Lord of the Rings meme and then you click it, and to click it, to see it, you have to re-download the app, and they get me every time. Warzel: It’s a gateway drug. Beck: Lord of the Rings memes are the gateway drug kids. But no, I noticed something happening maybe six-ish months ago when whenever I was on my last round of being on TikTok, which is: Every time I would go on there, I would get nothing but reels of “how to be offline more”, like “how to live more analog,” “how to heal your attention span” on this app where I was actively in the process of degrading my attention span. So I thought that irony was interesting, and so I think there was a shift that I was just sensing within myself, but also in conversations that I would have with people in real life and in what I was seeing online of people really trying to just be on their phones less, be on social media less. And I was curious why now, when obviously we’ve had smartphones for a very long time, we’ve had the internet for a very long time, we’ve had social media for a long time. Warzel: What is the answer to that? Why now? Beck: Why now? I think some of it is that we’ve had it for long enough that the shine’s off the apple, right? And I think some of it is a confluence of these different bigger conversations. Obviously, there’s like a big push by many to get kids off of social media, right? Or there’s lawsuits against Instagram, and What is Instagram doing to our mental health? And so I do think that those things have leaked down in some way, but also even TikTok, right, has been pretty popular for a few years. We’ve had a few years of living in this sort of algorithmically optimized short-form-video environment. And it’s gotten to the point where maybe people have had enough experience with it that they’re starting to see the effects in their own lives and like starting to question that rather than just, Oh, isn’t this fun? I can watch Lord of the Rings memes . And I think combining that with the sort of arrival of AI on the scene, right? And seeing all of these extreme stories about people replacing relationships with AI, using AI as a friend or a lover—God forbid—I think there’s been a sort of opposite, if not equal, reaction to valuing more the embodied world and the real social relationships that we had. So I think people are reacting in part to the sort of evolution of the internet culture and social-media environment and the arrival of this new technology that’s really like getting its little tendrils into every area of our lives. Warzel: So one of the episodes—to pivot here—explores nostalgia, which I think is a very big part of all of this hand-wringing that we are all personally going through, right? Is this moment different from others? Are we doing something uniquely awful to our brains that none of our ancestors ever did? And when you talk about nostalgia, there’s particularly a focus on young people who weren’t really around to have that pre-internet life. In that episode though, you have this moment where you describe a time that you got truly and deeply lost. And so it struck me that your co-host, who’s slightly younger than you, never had that experience. She’d never been an adult without a smartphone. And so what do you think is the value of being in a place where you don’t have a phone to save you? Are we losing something when we don’t experience that vulnerability? Beck: Yes and no. I do look back on it with a fondness. I would no longer—unless my phone died, I guess—I would no longer ever be in a position where I simply had to throw myself on the mercy of strangers and hope that they helped me. If I were lost somewhere, I can just follow the blue dot until I figured it out. And I don’t know that I yearn to go back to that. In some ways, that wasn’t very safe. I was like a young woman traveling alone in a country where I didn’t speak the language, and I had no idea where I was and no way to really communicate with anyone. I’m not mad that I have Google Maps and I have some sort of safety features to keep me safe when I go places. And I do think we have lost a little bit of something of just, kind of, being where you are and letting the experience be what it is. And those opportunities for connection, right? I would not ask someone for help. I would just use my phone. So I feel ambivalent about it. And I would say that, in fact, ambivalence is the primary emotion of the season and of just today’s technology. Warzel: So there’s this stat that you reference—because we’re talking a little bit about people who haven’t had access to a life without smartphones—and I found it honestly just bracing, maybe even troubling, but the stat is essentially that 60 percent of Gen Z wishes that they could return to a time before everyone was “plugged in.” And nostalgia’s a very common thing. You get into this in the episode. Everyone has nostalgia for some period of time. But Gen Z’s nostalgia for this time before they were alive, it seems like something else to me. Like it seems like a genuine indictment of this moment that we are in. How do you read that stat? What does that make you feel when you hear that? Beck: I take that status as not actually indicative of if you presented them with a time machine and were like, “You can go live in 1985,” that they would go in there and live in 1985. I don’t think they actually want to give up on all of the other things that have happened since then. But it’s just this sense of like, Something in my life isn’t working. I attribute it to this device , and it’s being expressed as like, I just wish we could go back . But I don’t think it actually means they wish they could go back. Warzel: Yeah. I think one thing that I’m trying to figure out is: Do you feel like it’s just an escapist phenomenon in that way, or just a coping mechanism? Or do you think it actually leads to or has the potential to lead to a genuine backlash or push or protest against some of this stuff. I think about just the physical-media boom, like a push to do some things in a more analog way, even if it is kind of “niche” or “hipster,” or whatever you wanna call it. Beck: Yeah, I feel like maybe I went into this thinking it is just kind of an escapist fantasy, in the way that somebody might be like, I should’ve been born in the 1920s. I would have made such a great flapper , or whatever it may be. But the expert who we interviewed for that episode, Clay Routledge, he studies nostalgia, and his whole take on nostalgia overall is that it’s about the future as much as it is about the past. So it’s not just warm feelings for the past and like, What a nice time I had doing whatever, but it’s also telling you something important about the way that you want to live now and going forward. And so, especially seeing what you’re talking about: the sort of rise in people buying physical media again, people giving up their smartphones for dumb phones. I do think it is inspiring some level of actual behavioral change. And even if you don’t go so far as to get a dumb phone and try to LARP your life like it’s the ’90s, I think it still tells you something important about what you value and maybe smaller shifts that you do want to make in how you relate to technology and how you set up your life. Warzel: If there’s one real theme of How to Touch Grass , I think it’s that the tools that we use change us, obviously, in these unexpected ways, right? Our habits, how we see ourselves, how we see other people, how we talk to each other—everything. And the show explores this from anxiety to body image. And I wanna play you another clip from your own show here. Sophie Gilbert: I don’t think anyone is supposed to see their own face as much as we do now. I think about this a lot, like how our ancestors would have felt like catching a glance at themselves in a lake. And instead we’re front-facing camera, front-facing camera, front-facing camera , and it’s weird. It’s warping our brains. Warzel: That was our fellow staff writer, Sophie Gilbert, talking to you. What strikes me a bit about being hyper-connected is that, in theory, the access to abundant information that we have should be a good thing, I think. And it just doesn’t seem to work that way in practice. Like the way that we can learn anything, but we tend to gravitate towards information that confirms our biases, right? And pushes us deeper down whatever rabbit hole. Or how we can learn anything about our bodies and then it pushes us to go and Google these things that lead to more and more anxiety. The thing that Sophie gets at in that clip, really, is something that you hear a lot of people say, which is, We were never supposed to have this much access to ourselves, other people, information , and yet we hold that up as: That’s the beauty of the internet. That’s the great thing—more, more, more, abundance, the Library of Alexandria at your fingertips, whatever, right? But what do you feel like this access is doing to people? Beck: I think what I’ve been thinking a lot about since wrapping up the interviews for that season is that there are costs to every way of living. And what is happening is that the design of our technology—the design of these apps of smartphones, or honestly the design of society in general right now—is pushing you to accept a certain set of costs and trade-offs. And that is: constant distraction and the slow degradation of your attention span and maybe some body-image problems in exchange for the most abundance of entertainment, connection, communication, relationships, information that you could possibly imagine. And that is a trade-off that you may decide is worth making, right? At this moment in time, maybe I’m waiting for the bus and it is worth it to me to degrade my attention span a little and be entertained. But are you actually consciously choosing those costs, or are you just sort of being pushed by default into making those trade-offs? And there are trade-offs to inserting more distance between yourself and your phone as well. The phone is kind of where the people are, and so if you want to be on your phone less, then maybe you are gonna be a little bit less connected to long-distance loved ones, or maybe you’re gonna have a harder time figuring out what is the weather today, or getting that information that you need right now about how to get into the concert venue. It’s like there are costs either way. However, all of society is kind of set up to push you towards one set of costs. And I think people are starting to question that a little bit. Warzel: Yeah, and I think if there’s an insidious part of the Big Tech experience, right, it is making people feel when they’re using these things like there aren’t any trade-offs. They are marketed as Connection is a universal good or This thing is a universal productivity increaser , and you should feel this way about them. Some of what we’re feeling in this moment, I think, is maybe not fully being gaslit, but you’re experiencing the trade-offs, the costs, and you’re sort of conditioned not to think that there are any. So you’re like, What’s wrong with me that I can’t get a handle on this, that I can’t get a handle on my attention span or feel this way? And I think it’s a bit of, like: No, no, no, no, no. You have to do that inventory of the give-and-take. And you also have to know that it’s not a fair fight and that’s okay. You just need to be armed with that information. I think that we’re not as much these days. Beck: Yeah. Well, I also think a lot about the way that—a lot of the response to this, a lot of the current movement to log off or do whatever is very draconian. It’s like, I’m getting rid of my phone and I’m getting a dumbphone, and I’m never gonna look at social media ever again . Because I think the reasonable alternative, unfortunately, is that you just kind of have to manage it forever. Like you said, the deck is stacked against you. These companies are not going to decide that they want less of your attention, wake up one morning and decide that they’ve had enough. And so it feels for a lot of people that the fantasy is to just completely leave it behind forever and walk into the sea and live an analog existence. And if you don’t want to live that way, or if it is not reasonable to live that way, which I think for most people it’s not, then unfortunately the answer is just kind of dealing with that push-and-pull and designing something—it’s very DIY, right?—it’s designing something for yourself with your phone, with your technology that works for you. And it requires kind of constant upkeep, constant management, and constant resistance of the forces that are trying to suck you in, and that’s kind of exhausting. Warzel: Yeah, absolutely. You devoted an episode to the ways that technology is changing the way that we learn. And I think that people can feel that disruption right now, especially with chatbots. I wanna play a clip from an interview you did with Michelle Miller, who’s a cognitive psychologist at Northern Arizona University. Michelle Miller: I think that teaching another human being how to do something, that is one of the highest and best expressions of humanity that there is. It’s one of the best and most positive ways that we interact with and contribute to one another. Odell: —actually, I’m saying Kill grass . No, I’m just kidding. ( Laughs. ) But the reason I think it became such a—that phrase caught on was because it’s just so obviously true. The obvious truth of it is, like, why it’s funny and annoying at the same time. Beck: Yeah. What is it that you think the natural world has to teach us about attention? Odell: Complexity, basically. Like, I think it’s a master class in complexity. It is kind of an antidote to the idea of the easy answer, which I think—I really blame Instagram for the oversimplification of political issues.Like, personally, that is just my ax to grind. And the idea that you could sort of absolve yourself by reposting something is just—yeah. It’s upsetting to me. But I think that there’s no easy answers to anything. Like, if you are a birder and you like birds, well, guess what? You’re gonna have to learn about trees. Beck: Mm-hmm. Odell: And then gonna have to learn about, like, seasons, and then, I don’t know, there’s just—everything is so tied to everything else, and there are so many things that are sort of, like, neither good nor bad or sort of arguable. We need lessons in that right now. Like, we need lessons in the sort of, like, Let me pick a point in space to look at, and then let me look at the context around that. Okay, now let me look at the context around that. And now you’ve sort of widened this whole ecosystem. I think the opposite of that is what happens online. Beck: So Jenny, if someone is just starting to rethink the relationship they have with their devices, what advice would you give them? Odell: Try to take an outsider’s perspective on yourself. I’m a big journaler, so I’ve journaled since I was a kid. So that would work for me. I would look at my phone, I would look at some stuff on my phone, and then I would just write down, kinda what it was and then how I felt about it. And I would be, like, brutally honest. Beck: Oh, man. Odell: Just pretend like you’re a scientist. And just talk to a friend about it. You could write it down, like, whatever. But, you know, I think there needs to be that, like, every so often you step to the side and you go, Okay, what did I just do? Like, Why did I do that? How did that make me feel? You can be super brief about it. Just do it for a week. Just see what it tells you. Beck: Yeah. Odell: Before you try to make any changes, because the danger is that a person feels shame, they feel that it’s bad. They’re like, Okay, I need to change this , and then they try really hard to change it, and then it doesn’t go the way they wanted, and then they feel more shame. And now it’s just, like, a spiral. Beck: Yeah. I think especially with attention for whatever reason, it does feel very shameful, this like, Oh, I can’t focus; I can’t pay attention. I can’t even, like, read a book without having the desire to pick up my phone. Odell: Yeah. And people think it means that they’re a bad person, and it doesn’t. You just gotta be patient and try a bunch of different things and maybe it’ll be more interesting than you think. [ Music ] Beck: Guys, huge news. Huge news. I locked my gym locker today. Nature is healing. I am the virus. For once in my goddamn life, I locked my gym locker. It is day 13. I was on the computer all day for work because computer is where the money comes from. You can still screen fatigue yourself. ( Laughs. ) The old-fashioned way. Captain’s log, the final full day of the experiment. Over the past two weeks, I read one full novel, I started two other books, I finished an audiobook, I crocheted a hat, I watched all of the first season of The Traitors . It’s not like I, you know, found myself with a magical abundance of time. I think it’s more like I just paid more attention and spent more time doing the things that I already like to do. That was time mostly well spent, so attention mostly well spent. Brennan: Julie, when you set out to go on this experiment you got in touch with one of the researchers from the 2025 study, Kostadin Kushlev from Georgetown University, who agreed to go over the results of your post-experiment attention test with us. And before we call him up, are you nervous about your results, not so nervous about these results? Will it mean less to you if your attention span didn’t change on paper? Beck: I mean, I guess I’m a little nervous. I mean, look, I am a nerd and I always wanna get an A+ on my projects. But I really do feel better, and if it’s just a placebo effect, well, a placebo effect is still an effect, right? Like, I’ll take it. Brennan: Okay, I’m gonna dial Kosta up. [ Phone ringing ] Kostadin Kushlev: Hello. Brennan: Hi, I’m Natalie. I’m Julie’s producer. I’m also gonna be sitting in on this call. Kushlev: Hi, Natalie. Beck: Hey, Kosta. It’s Julie. How are you? Kushlev: Pretty good. How are you doing? Beck: I’m doing okay! So, can we just dive right in? Kushlev: Yes. Beck: And tell me, before I started the experiment, how was my baseline attention span? Kushlev: So your score was about three, 3.02. Beck: Is that good? Good for a 35-year-old? Good, bad? Kushlev: That’s pretty good. Essentially, you did about how our participants did. It’s a little closer to the level you might see in young adulthood or for somebody in their 60s. ( Laughs. ) Beck: ( Laughs. ) Okay. Humbling. Humbling. Kushlev: Yes. Yes. But, you know, but once we get to your post score— Beck: Yes, let’s do it. Kushlev: — things really change. Beck: The big reveal. Kushlev: Yes. Beck: What changed? Kushlev: So your post score was actually hugely better. So it was 3.8. And that is much bigger improvement than we saw on average in our study. So your improvement is about four to five times bigger than what the average participant in our study gained. Brennan: Go Julie! Beck: Write it down, Natalie. Write it down. ( Laughs. ) Brennan: I’m taking notes. Kushlev: Yeah. So you did really well on that. Beck: Amazing, I think. Is 3.1 to 3.8 good? Have I reversed my cognitive decline? Or how would you characterize that? Kushlev: You’re basically off the charts. Beck: ( Laughs. ) Kushlev : But it might take a while to reap the benefits of this improved attention. Beck: Right. And it’ll probably go away if I just start scrolling Instagram again. Kushlev: Right. Yeah. Brennan: ( Laughs. ) Kushlev: It’s certainly not a permanent increase. But I do like to point out that, you know, just taking a two-week break and not even a complete break from your phone, just sort of like reducing your use, can actually improve that ability to sustain attention. Our lives are just like so tied to these devices, so sometimes the question might be: Have we like essentially permanently damaged our, you know— Beck: Yeah. Kushlev: —brains? Like, have we changed our neurobiology and so forth? And so this seems to suggest that no, there is a way out. So it might be worth doing some of those digital-detox interventions. [ Music ] Beck: Thank you so much, Kosta. It was great chatting with you! Kushlev: Alright, thank you, bye. Brennan: Bye! Brennan: Julie? Beck: Mm-hmm. Brennan: How do you feel about that? Beck: Unbearably smug. No, no, no. I’m just kidding. No, I feel relieved, honestly. Like, even if the true effect size isn’t as big as it seemed, ’cause I am just one person; it’s not, you know, a full scientific study— Brennan: Yeah. Beck: —it still feels really good to know that it’s possible to improve so quickly. Brennan: Right. Beck: So it’s actually kind of wild that you can do something as simple as this and, like, bounce back so quickly. Brennan: Are you going to keep using the Brick? Like, how are you feeling about—where’s your relationship at between you and your phone right now? Beck: My relationship with my phone is cordial. We’re not—it’s not warm— Brennan: ( Laughs. ) Beck : —but it’s not cold. We’re cordial. We’re friendly acquaintances. Brennan: That sounds like how people describe their exes. Beck: Yeah. And, well, we haven’t broken up. It really is—it’s a situationship— Brennan: Totally. Beck: —that is ongoing forever. No, I’m definitely gonna continue using the Brick, and I have been still. Twenty-three hours a day? You know, maybe not. Brennan: Yeah. Beck: I have been Bricking my phone, at a minimum, before bed, so I can’t doom scroll right before I sleep, and I can’t look at my emails or Instagram the second that I regain consciousness. So that does help. [ Music ] But I would say that throughout this, I kept thinking about my favorite poet, Mary Oliver, and one thing that she wrote was, “To pay attention, this is our endless and proper work.” Brennan: That’s beautiful. Beck: So this season, I think what I’ve learned is: Your attention is your life. And I think on some level I knew that already, but after this experiment, I’ve really been feeling it. Brennan: We started this season because we wanted to understand why so many people were feeling the pull to log off, right? We’ve explored a lot of the ways in which the internet can pull you into thoughtless patterns, whether it’s the way Instagram makes us feel bad about our bodies or the way that AI chatbots can send us into an anxious spiral. But it seems like what we are maybe actually looking for, right now, is ways to be more thoughtful. Beck: Yeah, I wanted to feel more thoughtful about my life. I wanted to not to feel as much like I’m literally giving my life away to things that I don’t even care about. I wanted to stop nickel-and-diming the moments of my life away. Brennan: Being intentional about where you give your attention. [ Music ] Beck: This episode was hosted by me, Julie Beck, and co-hosted and produced by Natalie Brennan, with production help from Elena Schwartz. Our editors are Claudine Ebeid and Jocelyn Frank. Fact-check by Gisela Salim-Peyer. Our engineers are Rob Smierciak and Miguel Carrascal. Rob also composed some of the music for this show. The executive producer of audio is Claudine Ebeid, and the managing editor of audio is Andrea Valdez. Warzel: Thank you again to my guest, Julie Beck. If you liked what you saw here, new episodes of Galaxy Brain drop every Friday. You can subscribe at the Atlantic’s YouTube channel or on Apple or Spotify or wherever it is that you are getting your podcast these days. And if you want to support this work and the work of my colleagues like Julie and Natalie, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. That’s TheAtlantic.com/Listener. Thanks so much, and I’ll see you on the internet. This episode of Galaxy Brain was produced by Hadley Robinson, video edited by Denny Thomas and engineered by Miguel Carrascal. items.title: SECP introduces unified framework for 'faster and easier' entry into Pakistan's capital market
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) has introduced a unified digital investor onboarding framework to make entry into Pakistan’s capital market “faster and easier by reducing repetitive verification, simplifying documentation and setting clear timelines for opening investor accounts”. The framework aims particularly to facilitate first-time and digital investors, with ‘Sehl/Sahulat’ accounts to be processed within one working day and normal accounts within two working days, according to an SECP statement issued on Friday. “Applicants will receive tracking IDs, while any deficiencies will be communicated within the prescribed timeframe and reasons for rejection provided in writing,” it stated. The statement said the initiative was part of the SECP’s broader drive to expand retail participation, particularly among young Pakistanis, and increase the country’s capital-market investor base to 2.5 million. “Our focus is to remove entry barriers and use technology to make the investor journey simpler, faster and more accessible,” SECP Chairman Dr Kabir Ahmed Sidhu was quoted as saying. “The objective is to unlock the significant untapped potential of Pakistan’s capital market by broadening participation, particularly among the youth, and building a deeper and more inclusive market,“ he elaborated. The framework standardises onboarding requirements across “securities brokers, asset management companies, insurers and other regulated intermediaries, creating a more consistent investor experience across the regulated financial sector,” the statement said. According to the SECP, the key feature of the framework is the elimination of repetitive customer verification. Where prescribed verification has already been completed by an eligible regulated financial institution or notified third party, intermediaries can rely on that verification instead of requiring investors to repeat the process. “The framework also enables API-based straight-through processing and digital onboarding, including instant UIN issuance and opening of CDC sub-accounts, reducing paperwork and manual intervention,” the SECP said. A few months ago, the government of Pakistan also established the Capital Market Development Fund (CMDF), aimed at promoting financial literacy, expanding financial inclusion and increasing retail investor participation in the capital markets across the country.

items.title: Garde à vue de Sébastien Delogu : l'affaire qui perturbe l'été idyllique des Insoumis
items.description: Le depute des Bouches-du-Rhone Sebastien Delogu a passe plusieurs heures en garde a vue le 27 août au commissariat central de Marseille. Sorti peu avant 23 heures par une porte derobee, accompagne de son avocat, il a rapidement remercie sur X ses soutiens ainsi que « les forces de l'ordre qui se sont comportees de maniere irreprochable ». Il a precise etre rentre chez lui pour se reposer et s'exprimer bientot. Versions contradictoires et plaintes croisees L'incident remonte au lundi 24 août. Trois policiers du Service interdepartemental de securisation des transports en commun cherchaient un suspect de vol de montre dans l'immeuble ou reside l'elu. Selon les agents, Delogu se serait oppose physiquement a leur entree, les traitant notamment de « bande de fatigues » ou de « trou du c*** », et aurait affirme « La Republique, c'est moi », celebre phrase assenee par Jean-Luc Melenchon lors d'une perquisition en octobre 2018. 🇫🇷 FLASH | Les images de l'altercation entre le député LFI Sébastien Delogu et des policiers à Marseille. pic.twitter.com/weBRqYREs6 https://t.co/RhC7upVxbJ — Cerfia (@CerfiaFR) August 26, 2026 Ils ont depose plainte pour outrage a personne depositaire de l'autorite publique. De son cote, le depute affirme que les policiers, en civil, n'avaient pas decline leur identite. Il decrit des insultes (« tu pues de la g*** », phrase qu'il avait lui-meme dite a une militante feministe quelques mois plus tot) et un coup sur la poitrine. Il a porte plainte contre X pour violences volontaires et saisi l'IGPN. La video qui circule est partielle et ne tranche pas le litige. Les reactions politique n'ont pas tarde et l'elu, qui n'etait pas present a la photo des cadres LFI lors de l'universite d'ete du mouvement a ete soutenu par des elus de son parti tandis que ses adversaires ont denonce son attitude vis-a-vis des policiers a l'image de l'eurodepute RN Matthieu Valet qui a dit son « soutien total aux 3 policiers » tandis que la ministre deleguee chargee de l'egalite entre les femmes et les hommes et de la Lutte contre les discriminations a declare le 28 août : « La France insoumise a mis la violence au cœur d'une strategie politique ». «La France insoumise a mis la violence au cœur d'une stratégie politique», alerte Aurore Bergé, ministre déléguée chargée de l'Égalité entre les femmes et les hommes et de la Lutte contre les discriminations, après la garde à vue de Sébastien Delogu, dans #LaGrandeInterview pic.twitter.com/CaW3lc3KZp — CNEWS (@CNEWS) August 28, 2026 L'elu, deja condamne en 2025 pour violences et convoque le 21 octobre dans une autre affaire, comparaîtra le 13 novembre devant le tribunal correctionnel de Marseille. Cet episode vient troubler un ete que les Insoumis esperaient plus serein, alors que la rentree politique approche et que son universite d'ete a ete un succes.

items.title: Urgent/ BCRG Vs Syndicat : le tribunal relaxe les trois syndicalistes et déboute le parquet et la partie civile
items.description: Le tribunal correctionnel de Kaloum a rendu ce vendredi 28 août 2026 sa décision dans l’affaire opposant trois membres de la délégation syndicale de la Banque centrale de la République de Guinée (BCRG) à Daouda Sankhon, aide de camp du gouverneur de l’institution. Poursuivis notamment pour des faits présumés d’« outrage à agent, violences et voies de fait », les trois syndicalistes ont finalement été renvoyés des fins de la poursuite et relaxés par le tribunal. Les charges jugées non constituées Dans sa décision, le tribunal a estimé que les éléments constitutifs du délit d’outrage, prévu par l’article 658 du Code pénal, n’étaient pas réunis à la charge des prévenus. Il a également considéré que les éléments constitutifs des faits de violences ou voies de fait, prévus par l’article 240 du Code pénal, n’étaient pas établis. Le tribunal a ainsi conclu qu’ « aucun acte matériel constitutif d'outrage ou de violence ou encore de voies de fait n'est établi ni personnellement imputable » aux prévenus. En conséquence, les trois syndicalistes ont été renvoyés des fins de la poursuite et relaxés. Le ministère public débouté de ses réquisitions Cette décision vient également contredire les réquisitions formulées la veille par le ministère public. Lors de l’audience du jeudi 27 août, le procureur Issouf Fofana avait requis que les trois prévenus soient déclarés coupables d’outrage à agent et condamnés chacun au paiement d’un million de francs guinéens d’amende. Le tribunal a finalement débouté le ministère public de ses réquisitions. La demande de 100 millions rejetée Sur l’action civile, le tribunal a reçu Daouda Sankhon en sa constitution de partie civile, tout en la déclarant mal fondée. Sa demande de condamnation des trois syndicalistes au paiement de 100 millions de francs guinéens à titre de dommages et intérêts a ainsi été rejetée. Le tribunal a également rejeté la demande de comparution formulée au cours de la procédure et mis les dépens à la charge de la partie civile. Retour sur les faits L’affaire remonte au 6 août 2026, lorsque plusieurs travailleurs de la BCRG, dont les trois prévenus, s’étaient rendus auprès du gouverneur Karamo Kaba pour faire entendre des revendications syndicales. Vêtus de rouge, les syndicalistes souhaitaient notamment obtenir une rencontre avec le gouverneur autour de leurs revendications portant sur leurs conditions de vie et de travail ainsi que sur la signature du protocole d’accord 2026. L’accès au bureau du gouverneur leur avait alors été refusé par son aide de camp, Daouda Sankhon, à l’origine de la plainte. À la barre, les trois prévenus avaient rejeté les accusations portées contre eux. Le plaignant avait, de son côté, affirmé que Momo Camara avait poussé la porte à deux reprises, tout en précisant que les syndicalistes ne l’avaient ni insulté ni touché. Après les réquisitions du parquet et les plaidoiries de la défense, le tribunal avait mis l’affaire en délibéré. Ce vendredi, il a finalement tranché en faveur des prévenus, en prononçant leur relaxe et en rejetant aussi bien les réquisitions du ministère public que la demande indemnitaire de la partie civile.

items.title: Warsh resalta su compromiso para reconducir la inflación al 2% y anuncia medidas si es necesario
items.description: Acaba de llegar y ya tiene enfrente una encrucijada de difícil resolución. Los inversores esperaban con atención el discurso del nuevo presidente de la Reserva Federal (Fed) de Estados Unidos, Kevin Warsh, de este viernes en el cónclave de banqueros centrales que cada verano se celebra en Jackson Hole, en las montañas de Wyoming. El recién llegado hereda un rompecabezas endemoniado. Unas previsiones de crecimiento repletas de dudas, con una guerra en Irán sin fecha de caducidad, una inflación por encima del objetivo del 2% y un mercado de la deuda en tensión es el cóctel con el que tiene que lidiar. Ante este complejo panorama, Warsh ha echado algo de luz sobre sus próximos pasos. items.title: 10 of 12 parties prequalified for Fesco privatisation, K-Electric withdraws
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The Privatisation Commission Board on Friday approved the prequalification of 10 out of 12 interested parties (IPs) for the sale of Faisalabad Electric Supply Company (Fesco), after K-Electric (KE) withdrew its papers and a lone Chinese firm failed to demonstrate sufficient interest in the competition. The development came after Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif directed the relevant authorities to adopt a “comprehensive strategy” earlier this month to attract international investors for the privatisation of state-owned power distribution companies (Discos) and complete the restructuring of the Privatisation Commission within one month. Informed sources said KE, the country’s only privatised power utility, had decided to withdraw rather than risk being disqualified due to the non-availability of its financial accounts for the past two years — a key requirement. They said the company would bid for another distribution company (Disco) as part of a consortium with Shahryar Chishti’s AsiaPak Investments, one of KE’s major shareholders. “K-Electric has withdrawn its Expression of Interest (EOI) for Fesco’s privatisation,” a KE spokesperson confirmed when contacted. He added that the decision was taken because the Disco’s audited financial statements were not yet available, pending finalisation of the company’s Multi-Year Tariff (MYT), which was beyond KE’s control. “We remain committed to pursuing opportunities that maximise value for our stakeholders“, he said. On the other hand, Jiang Xi Electric Power Construction of China did not meet the prequalification criteria, as it filed its EOI in Chinese rather than English on the last day of the deadline, despite repeated requests to submit it in English. The board meeting, presided over by Prime Minister’s Adviser on Privatisation and Privatisation Commission Chairman Muhammad Ali, approved all other prospective bidders for the next stage. The board was informed that a total of 12 EOIs had been received for Fesco. After evaluating the submissions against the approved prequalification criteria, the financial adviser recommended 10 IPs for prequalification. Three are from Turkiye — Aktor Elektrik Enerji Yatırımları San ve Tic AŞ, Genvera Enerji AŞ (Celik Group) and Cengiz Enerji Sanayii ve Ticaret AŞ. The remaining seven Pakistani groups are Engro Energy Limited; Sapphire Fibres Limited, Hub Power Holdings, Lucky Cement and Metro Ventures; Shirazi Investments (Pvt) Limited (Atlas Group); Maple Leaf Cement and Kohinoor Textile; the Pakgen Limited Consortium, comprising Nishat Mills, Nishat Power, Nishat Chunian, Lalpir, Pak Elektron Ltd and Kohinoor Energy; and Artistic Milliners (Private) Limited. The prequalified parties will now proceed to the next stage of the transaction in accordance with the approved process, including access to the Virtual Data Room (VDR) for detailed buy-side due diligence. The board also approved the reconstitution of its Audit and Risk, Human Resources, Investment and Legal committees. The commission said the privatisation aims to improve operational efficiency, modernise distribution infrastructure, strengthen customer service, reduce losses and support a more financially sustainable power sector. Over time, these measures will help create the conditions for more competitive electricity distribution and affordable, reliable power for consumers, it added. Fesco is among the three electricity distribution companies in Disco Batch-I privatisation, alongside Gujranwala Electric Power Company ( Gepco ), which attracted 11 EOIs, most of them also in the run for Fesco and Islamabad Electric Supply Company (Iesco). The deadline for submission of EOIs for Iesco is September 7, 2026. The Privatisation Commission said it would ensure an open, transparent and competitive privatisation process, undertaken in the public interest and in support of the federal government’s wider power-sector reform agenda. Earlier this week, the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority notified sweeping guaranteed performance and overall performance standards for all Discos after more than two decades, to ensure compliance even after going into private hands under the ongoing privatisation process. The new Performance Standards (Distribution) Regulations 2026, issued by the regulator after almost two years of consultations with stakeholders, replace the Discos Performance Rules 2005. Under the new standards, utilities will, for the first time, face mandatory consumer compensation, besides heavy fines, if they fail to meet strict deadlines for restoring power after blackouts, replacing faulty meters, addressing voltage fluctuations, providing new connections and other services.

Attention, rien ne confirme l’arrestation de Mahmoud Dicko à Alger
items.description: Une publication devenue virale sur TikTok affirme que l'imam Mahmoud Dicko « a ete arrete a l'aeroport international Houari-Boumediene d'Alger, puis place en residence surveillee par les autorites algeriennes ». Aucune source officielle consultee par notre redaction ne confirme cette information. Depuis mardi 25 août, une publication largement relayee sur TikTok affirme que l'imam Mahmoud Dicko a ete « arrete a son arrivee a l'aeroport international Houari-Boumediene d'Alger ». Selon son auteur, l'imam aurait ensuite ete place en residence surveillee par les autorites algeriennes. La publication evoque egalement un possible « refoulement de l'imam vers le Mali ». La video comptabilisait plus de 137 000 vues et des milliers d'interactions au moment de notre verification. Ces chiffres peuvent toutefois evoluer rapidement. Aucune confirmation de l'arrestation Apres recherches, recoupements et verifications, aucune source officielle consultee ne confirme l'arrestation de Mahmoud Dicko a Alger. Notre redaction a egalement contacte plusieurs personnes proches de l'imam. Aucune n'a confirme son arrestation ni un eventuel placement en residence surveillee. a ce stade, rien ne permet donc d'affirmer que Mahmoud Dicko a ete arrete a Alger ou place en residence surveillee par les autorites algeriennes. Une information a prendre avec prudence Le nombre de vues ou d'interactions d'une publication sur les reseaux sociaux ne constitue pas une preuve de la veracite de l'information qu'elle diffuse. En l'absence de confirmation officielle ou de source fiable permettant d'etayer ces affirmations, cette publication doit etre prise avec des pincettes. Avant de partager une information virale, il est preferable d'en verifier l'origine et de rechercher une confirmation aupres de sources fiables. Lire aussi : Cette video ne montre pas une attaque du JNIM contre une station-service a Badalabougou L’article Attention, rien ne confirme l’arrestation de Mahmoud Dicko à Alger est apparu en premier sur Studio Tamani - Informations, débats, magazines : toute l’actualité du Mali, en 5 langues .

items.title: ​ Axe AIBD-Dakar : la circulation totalement paralysée par un grave carambolage
items.description: Un spectaculaire carambolage impliquant plusieurs véhicules s'est produit ce vendredi 28 août sur l'autoroute à péage reliant l'Aéroport international Blaise Diagne (AIBD) à Dakar. L'accident a entraîné la fermeture complète du tronçon situé entre Toglou et Sébikotane, plongeant la zone dans une congestion majeure. Aux alentours de 11 h 30, les autorités sur place signalaient un embouteillage s'étirant sur près de 4 kilomètres. La gravité des collisions et l'ampleur du bouchon compliquent fortement la progression des équipes d'intervention et des secours. Face à cette paralysie du trafic, les services de régulation de la circulation invitent instamment les usagers en provenance de l'AIBD ou du réseau autoroutier Segea à emprunter la sortie n° 13 afin de contourner le secteur via la Route Nationale. Il est vivement conseillé aux automobilistes de faire preuve de vigilance et de différer ou d'anticiper l'ensemble de leurs déplacements dans la zone.

items.title: Doufelgou/santé : Un atelier de cadrage pour renforcer la lutte contre les VBG
items.description: Niamtougou, 28 août (ATOP) – Un atelier de cadrage sur le projet de création et d’opérationnalisation d’un cadre de coordination multisectoriel et de mobilisation communautaire pour lutter contre les Violences basées sur le genre (VBG) s’est tenu le vendredi 28 août à Niamtougou. L’initiative s’inscrit dans la mise en œuvre des activités du Plan de développement communal (PDC) de Doufelgou 1. Ce projet se déroule sur trois mois (août en octobre) et bénéficie de l’appui financier la coopération allemande à travers la troisième phase du Programme Santé (ProSanté III) mise en œuvre par la GIZ. Présentation du projet Le but est de renforcer, de manière coordonnée et participative, les interventions dans les domaines du genre, de la lutte contre les VBG, de la santé sexuelle et reproductive, de la nutrition et de la santé communautaire. Il s’agit de rendre opérationnel un cadre de coordination multisectoriel réunissant les acteurs institutionnels, les organisations de la société civile et les leaders communautaires. Le dispositif prévoit des rencontres trimestrielles, la formation des leaders communautaires sur la prévention des VBG et les droits sexuels et reproductifs. Il concerne aussi la nutrition et la santé communautaire, ainsi que des actions de sensibilisation sur les normes culturelles néfastes afin de favoriser un changement durable des comportements. Des activités, entre autres, des campagnes de sensibilisation communautaire, des causeries éducatives, des débats publics et des sessions de renforcement de capacités sont prévues dans le programme. Des messages de prévention seront également diffusés à travers les radios locales, le théâtre-forum, l’affichage et les médias sociaux. La rencontre a permis aux parties prenantes de mieux appréhender le contexte et les enjeux du projet, mettant l’accent sur la nécessité d’une synergie d’action entre les secteurs de la santé, de la justice, des affaires sociales et de la sécurité. L’implication des communautés à la base devra également contribuer à déconstruire les tabous et à instaurer un environnement protecteur. Le maire de la commune, Massoka Barima, a relevé la persistance des VBG, des mariages précoces, des grossesses non désirées et de certaines normes socioculturelles néfastes, qui affectent particulièrement les femmes, les adolescentes et les groupes vulnérables. Selon lui, le projet entend contribuer à remédier au manque de synergie entre les différents intervenants sur le terrain. M. Massoka a exhorté les chefs traditionnels et les autorités locales à veiller au respect des futures dispositions, tout en appelant à un encadrement accru de la jeunesse. Il a également invité le conseil municipal à envisager des dispositions réglementaires visant à mieux protéger les jeunes et à promouvoir un cadre social sain. La rencontre a réuni des chefs traditionnels, des membres des comités cantonaux et villageois de développement (CCD et CVD), des représentants des confessions religieuses, des organisations de la société civile ainsi que des syndicats des corps de métiers. ATOP/SG/TAL/DHK

items.title: The Limits of Yayoi Kusama’s Infinity
items.description: Years before the polka-dotted pumpkins, before the Instagrammable Infinity Mirror Rooms, Yayoi Kusama made art that was charged with oppositional energy. Her performances, in which she painted dots onto the naked bodies of her collaborators, were an expression of ’60s counterculture. They were protests against the Vietnam War, rebukes to the art market. Her Accumulations—soft sculptures of furniture or common household items covered in stuffed, handsewn penis shapes—were hilarious critiques of phallocentrism and early examples of feminist art. Kusama was, in other words, part of the artistic avant-garde. Her death, at 97, is a cold reminder that the avant-garde no longer exists. You could point to Andy Warhol, Jeff Koons, Takashi Murakami, or Keith Haring, but in many ways, no one epitomizes the collapse of the avant-garde more vividly than Kusama. I’m mostly a fan of her work. It’s very hard not to like her Infinity Mirror Room installations and playful gourds, and not to smile when you see Kusama’s endearing face framed by her signature brightly colored bobbed wig. But at a certain point, you can’t help but feel that she stopped being an artist and chose instead to become a highly profitable brand. In death as in life, her name bestrides a tightly managed, commercially successful global enterprise with diverse revenue streams, including high-profile partnerships with luxury labels, licensed merchandise, and strictly managed intellectual-property protection. Kusama’s large-scale sculptures and immersive installations break attendance records at museums and galleries around the world, and her works regularly set records at auction. In her final years, she was one of the world’s top-selling contemporary artists. Decades before all of that, though, Kusama was a creative maverick. After moving to New York from Tokyo in the late 1950s, she became a pioneer of both pop art and minimalism, then a key figure in performance art. She called her early breakthrough paintings—expansive, swirling fields of tightly packed dots—Infinity Nets. Before even Andy Warhol (although after Marcel Duchamp), she made her own persona an expression of her art, paving the way for such figures as Gilbert and George, the British-artist duo who made life itself a performance. Seymour Wally / NY Daily News / Getty Yayoi Kusama paints Kent Feathergill in 1967. Kusama’s artworks had countercultural energy. They fought against cliché. They critiqued patriarchy. They broke down starchy inhibitions and wobbled magnificently on the edge of the rational. They tried, in other words, to open up new ways of seeing. That was what the avant-garde was all about: It was an attempt to see the world afresh. For many of its leading figures, from the Impressionists in the 1870s to conceptual artists a century later, this also meant proposing new and better solutions to the problem of how to be and how to live together. These proposals, many times rooted in sympathy and love, were presented as alternatives to the political structures and market logic that had so often led to war, exploitation, hopelessness, and suffering. Even when attempts to turn these imagined alternatives into reality failed—and often dismally—the avant-garde stood in a clear relationship to modernity’s traumas. It was like the whistle cap in the spout of a boiling kettle: both a release of suppressed pressures (psychic and cultural) and an alarm. But society got sick of hearing the alarm. And the kettle got tired of whistling. Kusama, having experienced a period of art-world success, had her own breakdown after returning to Tokyo permanently in 1973. Two years later, she checked herself in to a psychiatric institution, where she became a permanent resident from 1977 until her death. The institution was within walking distance of her multistory studio. [ Read: An artist for the Instagram age ] Her psychic travails had to do with her upbringing (she had an authoritarian mother and an unfaithful father), which left her afraid of sex and intimacy. She suffered from severe audiovisual hallucinations, in which she would see flashing lights, auras, and dense fields of dots. She fell into deep episodes of clinical depression and attempted suicide twice. When Kusama reemerged as an active artist in 1989, she and her supporters presented her mental-health issues not just as an important aspect of her personal story but as part of the energy that fueled her artwork. All of this was healthy frankness, but it also undoubtedly enhanced her work’s reception. People could relate to the idea of creativity as a function of—and therapy for—mental illness. Kusama and her promoters emphasized the link, tapping into narratives about the artist as a suffering visionary that went back to Van Gogh and even earlier artists (including such figures as Piero di Cosimo, Caravaggio, and Rosso Fiorentino) whose artistic brilliance was linked to their strange behavior and (perhaps) mental instability. In the 20th century, the idea of a connection between creativity and interior turmoil was taken up with renewed gusto, and the category of outsider art (or art brut) was established. Outsider artists could reconnect us to the amputated life of the emotions, re-enchanting a world diagnosed by Max Weber, in 1917, as disenchanted. Kusama was one of many artists who swam with these currents. She talked about her repeating dots as an expression of an inclination toward “self-obliteration”—an urge to dissolve into forever-expanding patterns. The idea sounded at once mystical, therapeutic, and nightmarish. The idea that it might be all three only increased her appeal. Christopher Furlong / Getty The immersive exhibition “You, Me and the Balloons” in Manchester, England, in 2023 This second phase of Kusama’s art-world success far surpassed the first, proving, among other things, that you didn’t need to be in New York for your career to go gangbusters. She became one of the most popular artists on Earth. For museums struggling with attendances, she guaranteed box-office bonanzas. Her zany, luridly wigged persona helped dismantle the intimidation factor that prevents many people from relating to art and museums. Her work’s upbeat vibes and instant recognizability (spotted pumpkins!) were huge factors in her popularity. They made it easy to let go of the idea that you had to have prior knowledge or be somehow “initiated” into art before you could enjoy it. Jim Dyson / Getty One of the artist’s Infinity Mirror Rooms in 2008 in Liverpool, England But the speed with which Kusama converted her popularity into massive commercial success was sobering, if only because it seemed to signal her total co-option by the market. A turning point came in 2012, when the luxury-goods brand LVMH, under the creative direction of Marc Jacobs, incorporated Kusama’s polka dots into its clothing lines, adorning stores all around the world with her designs. As Georgina Adam reported in her 2014 book, Big Bucks: The Explosion of the Art Market in the 21st Century , the collaboration caused sales of Kusama’s work to take off and exposed her to audiences she would have never reached otherwise. From that point on, Kusama’s absorbing and fresh art, once charged by avant-garde energies, became more or less a meaning-free expression of market principles, an exercise in branding. She soon became a social-media phenomenon—the world’s most Instagrammable artist. Crowds waited in long lines just to spend 30 or 90 seconds in her Infinity Mirror Rooms taking selfies. Kusama’s talk of self-obliteration sounds vaguely Buddhist or Taoist. But I suspect it’s more clearly seen, in the late phase of Kusama’s career, as pure capitalism at work—a function of the same logic relied on by Big Tech as it converts the liberating potential of the internet into addiction, polarization, and advertising revenue, and a drastic narrowing of human potential. You will no longer need an inner life , says this logic. You will no longer even be you. You will be data points and dollar signs. You will be ubiquitous, self-obliterating dots. Kusama also achieved something that has eluded other artists who were co-opted by commerce and converted avant-garde energies into branding, including Warhol, Haring, Koons, and Murakami. The artist—an adorable maker of giant spotted pumpkins who lived in a psychiatric institution—became beyond criticism. You could no more criticize her than you could a grandmother giving a teddy bear to an orphan. Chesnot / Getty The headquarters of the Maison Louis Vuitton in 2023 in Paris, France I have almost always felt delight when I’ve entered one of Kusama’s Infinity Mirror Rooms or encountered her pumpkins. But I smell something rotten behind their sameness and ubiquity. Successful branding is exactly what art at its best is not: a form of general seduction rather than specific engagement. I prefer the earlier Kusama, the artist of extraordinary boldness, who carved out thrilling new possibilities for art in a hostile, male-dominated field. For this, she paid a heavy personal price. But it didn’t stop her from making art that felt specific to her, art targeted directly at you and me.

items.title: Quelles sont les leçons de la guerre en Ukraine pour l’Armée populaire de libération ?
items.description: La Chine est un soutien clef de la Russie dans sa guerre contre l'Ukraine, en lui fournissant notamment des composants destinés à la fabrication de drones et en permettant l'utilisation militaire de biens à double usage, des technologies avancées essentielles au développement, à la production ou à l'utilisation des systèmes militaires. Mais l’Armée populaire de libération (APL) suit également de près le front. Cela fait en effet deux ans que des soldats chinois se forment au pilotage de drones et au combat urbain dans un complexe militaire de Volgograd, dans le sud-ouest de la Russie China is gaining troubling military know-how from Russia », The Economist , 23 juillet 2026.'> 1 . La Chine, qui n’a pas mené de réelle guerre depuis un conflit frontalier d’un mois avec le Vietnam, en 1979, cherche à compenser son manque d’expérience au combat en tirant profit de son partenariat avec la Russie. Pékin s'intéresse notamment à la lutte anti-drone menée par la marine russe en mer Noire, qui pourrait lui donner un avantage en cas d’invasion ou d'imposition de blocus naval autour de Taïwan. Une série d'éditoriaux récemment publiés dans le Quotidien de l'APL, le journal officiel de l'armée chinoise, suggère que Pékin a tiré plusieurs enseignements de la guerre en Ukraine. Dans un article publié le 16 août, un auteur appelle ainsi à « placer le développement de forces de combat anti-systèmes sans pilote au rang de priorité stratégique majeure et de le promouvoir de manière intégrée, en privilégiant la conception de pointe, les systèmes d'équipements et un entraînement au combat réaliste, afin de prendre l'initiative dans la guerre intelligente » 挑灯看剑丨把准反无人作战力量建设着力点 », 解放军报, 16 août 2026.'> 2 . Selon un autre auteur, l’essor de l’IA, du big data a donné naissance à « un nouveau paradigme », en faisant de l'innovation tactique le principal moteur de développement de nouveaux équipements. Alors que, durant les précédents conflits du XXe siècle, « les conditions matérielles et technologiques déterminaient les limites de la guerre », ce sont désormais les besoins tactiques qui dictent les spécifications techniques des équipements. L'armée ne se contente ainsi plus de « se battre avec l'arme qu'elle a », mais « fabrique l'arme pour la guerre qu'elle mène ». La majeure des enseignements tactiques abordés par les auteurs se concentrent sur l’utilisation de l’intelligence artificielle, de la rapidité du cycle d’innovation, de l’organisation des structures d’approvisionnement et de la collecte de données sur le champ de bataille. Selon l’Institute for the Study of War, l’APL considère la guerre en Ukraine « comme une phase transitoire de la guerre moderne » qui cédera la place à une guerre « intelligente », dominée par l’IA et les essaims de drones. La technologie a déjà fait l’objet de plusieurs essais en conditions réelles en Ukraine, avec le système « Pasika », développé par l’entreprise ukrainienne Sine Engineering. Celui-ci vise à permettre à un seul opérateur de piloter plusieurs drones simultanément, qui agiraient comme un escadron : un « essaim » pouvant compter jusqu’à 100 engins évoluant sur terre, en mer et dans les airs « comme une seule unité ». La Chine a déjà annoncé développer un « vaisseau-mère », le Jiutan , capable de transporter jusqu’à 100 drones sur une distance de plusieurs milliers de kilomètres au sein d’une structure alvéolaire. L’article Quelles sont les leçons de la guerre en Ukraine pour l’Armée populaire de libération ? est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Ouagadougou : Près de 2 000 animaux mis en fourrière en trois mois
items.description: La divagation des animaux continue de poser des problèmes de sécurité et de salubrité à Ouagadougou. Entre juin et août 2026, environ 2 000 bovins, chevaux, ovins et caprins ont été conduits en fourrière lors des opérations menées par la Police municipale dans différents quartiers de la capitale. À Ouagadougou comme dans d'autres villes du Burkina Faso, il n’est pas rare de croiser, au détour d’une rue, un troupeau de bœufs avançant tranquillement entre les habitations, quelques moutons qui traversent la route sans regarder à gauche et à droite ou encore un âne ou un cheval qui semble avoir choisi lui-même son itinéraire. En cette saison pluvieuse, où la végétation reprend ses droits dans plusieurs espaces de la ville, certains animaux profitent ainsi des pâturages disponibles pour s’éloigner des concessions. Pour les propriétaires qui les laissent sortir paître, ces déplacements peuvent paraître ordinaires. Dans les rues de la capitale, ils deviennent cependant une source de préoccupations lorsqu’ils se font sans surveillance. Risques d’accidents, nuisances, dégradation des espaces verts et problèmes de salubrité figurent parmi les conséquences relevées par les services municipaux. Face à la persistance du phénomène, la Direction de la Police de la Salubrité et de la Tranquillité Urbaine (DPSTU) de la Police municipale de Ouagadougou a intensifié ses opérations au cours de la saison pluvieuse. Elle mène donc des opérations quotidiennes dans différents quartiers afin de retirer les animaux en divagation et de les conduire en fourrière. Entre juin et août 2026, environ 2 000 animaux ont ainsi été mis en fourrière dans différents quartiers de la capitale. Il s’agit notamment de bovins, de chevaux, d’ovins et de caprins. Une question de sécurité et de salubrité Au-delà de leur présence dans les rues, la divagation des animaux peut représenter un risque pour les usagers. La circulation de bovins, de chevaux ou de petits ruminants sur les voies peut notamment occasionner des accidents. La Police municipale rappelle aux propriétaires d’animaux la nécessité de prendre les dispositions nécessaires pour éviter leur divagation dans la ville. Elle rappelle également que cette question est encadrée par des textes, notamment la Loi n°022-2005/AN portant Code de l’hygiène publique au Burkina Faso et l’Arrêté n°97-027/MATS/PKAD/CO prescrivant les mesures d’hygiène et de salubrité dans la Ville de Ouagadougou. Josué TIENDREBEOGO Faso7 L’article Ouagadougou : Près de 2 000 animaux mis en fourrière en trois mois est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.description: BURKINA -GOURMA -ASSAINISSEMENT-DESHERBAGE Gourma : Une quarantaine de membres d’associations assainissent la cour et la devanture du haut-commissariat du Gourma Fada N’Gourma, 27 août 2026 (AIB)-Une quarantaine de membres des associations « Tin Taani Fi » et « Yanyenma » ont bravé la pluie, le jeudi 27 août 2026, pour mener une opération de salubrité au Haut-commissariat de la province du Gourma. Les participants ont procédé au désherbage et à l’assainissement des locaux et de la cour du Haut-commissariat du Gourma. L’initiative a été saluée par le Haut-commissaire de la province du Gourma, Silas Nacanabo. Mobilisés dès les premières heures de la journée du jeudi 27 août 2026, les bénévoles ont procédé au désherbage complet et au nettoyage de la cour intérieure ainsi que la devanture des locaux du Haut-commissariat du Gourma. Cette action d'assainissement a été conduite conjointement par l'association « Tin Taani Fi », dirigée par sa présidente, Noumpoa Tankoano, et l'association « Yanyenma », par son président, Yombo David Diakouma. Présent pour constater le déroulement des travaux, le Haut-commissaire de la province du Gourma, Silas Nacanabo, a exprimé sa gratitude aux participants pour cette mobilisation patriotique. L'autorité provinciale a vivement salué cet acte citoyen et a souligné qu'il permet d'offrir un cadre de travail propre et sain, au bénéfice des agents de l'administration et des usagers du service public. Agence d’information du Burkina KAC/HB/OO

items.title: Décentralisation : La commune Bas-Mono 1 entame l’élaboration de son PDC
items.description: Afagnan, 28 août (ATOP) – Le processus d’élaboration du Plan de développement communal (PDC) de la commune Bas-Mono 1 a été lancé, le jeudi 27 août à Afagnan. Cette activité s’inscrit dans le cadre de la mise en œuvre du processus de décentralisation pour un développement local durable et harmonieux des communautés. L’objectif est de mobiliser la population pour leur adhésion au processus. Le PDC est un document stratégique, indispensable pour la planification des actions afin de promouvoir un meilleur cadre de vie et améliorer les services sociaux de base aux communautés. C’est un outil destiné à orienter les actions et les investissements de la commune au cours des prochaines années. La rencontre a permis aux différents acteurs impliqués de prendre contact et de mettre en place les différents comités spécialisés chargés de conduire le processus d’élaboration du PDC. Les travaux d’élaboration vont s’étendre sur une durée de 6 à 8 mois, au terme de laquelle, la commune disposera d’un cadre de référence permettant de mieux planifier ses priorités et ses actions de développement. A travers cette démarche, la commune entend ainsi se doter d’une vision concertée de son développement en tenant compte des besoins et aspirations des populations. Le 2 ème adjoint au maire, Faustin Akakpo a relevé l’importance du PDC qui permettra à la mairie de relever les défis pour satisfaire les besoins des populations. Il a exhorté les acteurs et les populations à s’impliquer davantage dans la mise en œuvre du processus en vue de son heureux aboutissement. ATOP /DK/BA

items.title: 'No oath, no membership': ECP withdraws notification for Senate by-poll on seat won by PTI's Murad Saeed
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) on Friday formally withdrew its April 2 notification for the by-election programme for a general Senate seat from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which it had earlier declared vacant following the disqualification of PTI senator-elect Murad Saeed. In a notification, the ECP withdrew the election programme issued under its April 2 notification to “fill one general seat” in the Senate from KP, in pursuance of an order dated Aug 20. The withdrawal came a week after critics accused the ECP of assuming the role of a court by interpreting the Constitution to hold that no lawful vacancy had been created. Senate elections for 11 vacant seats from KP were held on July 21 last year. Saeed was declared a returned candidate for a general seat on July 24, 2025. However, on March 7 this year, Saeed was convicted by Rawalpindi’s Anti-Terrorism Court-I and sentenced to 10 years of imprisonment in the State vs Asim Rehman case, and on March 25, the commission determined that Saeed had been disqualified under Article 63(1)(h) of the Constitution. His seat was accordingly declared vacant. The by-poll was fixed for April 23 in the KP Assembly, but the process was halted after a petition was filed by PML-N MPA Jalal Khan, who argued that no lawful vacancy existed to justify the by-election. No oath, no membership, commission says In its detailed order, the ECP held that a clear constitutional distinction existed between a “returned candidate” and a “Member of Parliament”. “The publication of such notification signifies the conclusion of the electoral process to the extent of declaring a person as the returned candidate. However, such declaration, by itself, does not confer upon the returned candidate the constitutional status of a member of the Majlis-i-Shoora (Parliament),” the order states. Citing Article 255(3), the commission noted: “Where a person is required by the Constitution to make an oath before he enters upon an office, he shall be deemed to have entered upon the office on the day on which he makes the oath.” It further referred to Article 65, which bars a person from sitting or voting “until he has made before the House oath in the form set out in the Third Schedule”. The ECP noted the significance of the deliberate use of the expression “person elected” instead of “Member” in Article 65, saying that it demonstrated that “the Constitution itself recognises a distinction” between a person who had been elected or returned, and a person who had acquired the status of a member. Until the administration of the prescribed oath, a returned candidate remains a person elected to the House and does not attain the constitutional status of a Member,” the order reads. The ECP also interpreted Article 64 and Article 63(1) to mean that resignation or disqualification leading to a vacancy applied only to a person who had already acquired membership. “Therefore, the question of a seat becoming vacant arises only after the constitutional relationship of membership has been established,” it said. On Article 63(1)(h), the commission said clauses (g) and (h) “must be read in conjunction with the expression ‘from being a member’, as these provisions relate to circumstances where an existing member incurs a disqualification affecting his continuance in office”. The order concluded that a person could not be declared to have lost a seat which he had never occupied as a member, nor could a vacancy arise “in respect of a seat where the constitutional status of membership was never acquired”. “The commission is of the considered view that, notwithstanding the conviction of Murad Saeed, he has not yet acquired the status of a Member of Parliament; therefore, no lawful vacancy has arisen in respect of the said seat,” it said, adding that the question of holding a by-election therefore did not arise. Accordingly, the commission accepted the application and withdrew the April 2 election programme. Although the notification to withdraw the election programme after around five months is available on ECP’s official website, the order it was based on is not available.

items.title: Gourma/Faso Mêbo : L’Entreprise Tienu Sela offre du carburant et de l’eau minérale à l’antenne régionale
items.description: BURKINA-GOURMA-CONTRIBUTION-FASO-MEBO Gourma/Faso Mêbo : L’Entreprise Tienu Sela offre du carburant et de l’eau minérale à l’antenne régionale Fada N’Gourma, 28 août 2026 (AIB)-Le Président-directeur général (PDG) de l’Entreprise Tienu Sela, Amos Djolgou, accompagné de son personnel, a fait un don de 100 litres de gasoil et de 30 packs d’eau minérale ce vendredi 28 août 2026 à Fada N’Gourma, à l’Agence Faso Mêbo. L'équipe a également participé aux travaux de confection des pavés. La mobilisation citoyenne autour de l’Agence Faso Mêbo se poursuit dans la région du Goulmou. L’Entreprise Tienu Sela a concrétisé son engagement civique à travers un appui matériel composé de 100 litres de gasoil et de 30 paquets d’eau minérale, destinés à soutenir les équipes de terrain engagées dans l’embellissement et l’assainissement de la ville de Fada N’Gourma. Au-delà de la remise symbolique de ce don, le Président-directeur général (PDG) de l’Entreprise Tienu Sela, Amos Djolgou et ses collaborateurs ont participé à la confection des pavés sur le site des travaux. « Je salue vraiment le président camarade, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, pour l’initiative Faso Mêbo. Le travail que j’ai vu sur le terrain me réconforte très bien », a déclaré M. Djolgou. Il a salué l'action du coordinateur local et la propreté remarquable insufflée à la cité de Yendabili. Ce geste est la deuxième contribution de l’Entreprise Tienu Sela en faveur de cette initiative présidentielle. Au regard de l'impact des chantiers en cours, le premier responsable de l'entreprise a affirmé se préparer pour d’autres actions à venir. S'adressant aux citoyens, Amos Djolgou les a invités à visiter les chantiers de Faso Mêbo pour constater les réalités de terrain. « C’est notre pays, ce n’est personne d’autre qui viendra le construire à notre place », a-t-il rappelé. Agence d’information du Burkina KAC/HB/OO

items.title: Mali : une session spéciale d’examens de DEF pour les candidats de Kidal
items.description: a Kidal, 64 candidats au DEF, diplome d'etudes fondamentales, auront une nouvelle chance. Le ministere de l'education nationale prevoit une session speciale du 14 au 16 septembre, apres leur absence a la session de juin pour des raisons securitaires. Une nouvelle chance pour les candidats au DEF de Kidal. Le ministere de l'education nationale annonce une session speciale du 14 au 16 septembre 2026. Elle concerne 64 candidats de l'academie de Kidal qui n'avaient pas pu composer lors de la session ordinaire de juin, en raison de l'insecurite. Delocalisation des centres de Kidal lors des examens Les violences survenues le 25 avril dernier avaient provoque le deplacement de nombreux habitants. Les centres d'examen avaient alors ete delocalises a Gao et Menaka, mais la plupart des candidats n'avaient pas pu rejoindre ces centres. a Menaka, seuls 28 eleves sur 80 avaient finalement compose. Un cri de cœur attendu Face a cette situation, des organisations de la societe civile, ainsi que la Federation nationale de l'education, des sports, des arts, de la recherche et de la culture de Kidal, FENAREC-Kidal, avaient plaide pour une session speciale. Une demande desormais prise en compte par le ministere de l'education nationale. items.title: TPI de Kaloum : les trois leaders syndicaux de la BCRG renvoyés des fins de la poursuite
items.description: La décision dans l’affaire opposant le ministère public aux trois leaders syndicaux de la Banque centrale de la République de Guinée (BCRG) est tombée ce vendredi 28 août 2026 devant le tribunal correctionnel de Kaloum. Les prévenus, Aboubacar Sidiki Camara, secrétaire général adjoint du syndicat de la BCRG, Aboubacar Yansané, chargé de la santé, de la sécurité et de l’hygiène au travail au sein du syndicat de la BCRG, et Momo Camara, chargé des affaires sociales du syndicat de la BCRG, étaient poursuivis pour des faits d’« outrage à agent, violences et voies de fait », à la requête de l’adjudant-chef Daouda Sankhon, aide de camp du gouverneur de la BCRG, Karamo Kaba. Les faits remontent au 6 août dernier, lors d’un mouvement de revendication du syndicat portant notamment sur la prime scolaire destinée au personnel afin de contribuer à la scolarisation de leurs enfants. À l’audience de ce vendredi, le tribunal a déclaré les trois prévenus non coupables des faits qui leur étaient reprochés et les a renvoyés des fins de la poursuite pour délit non constitué. La juridiction a également débouté le ministère public ainsi que la partie civile de leurs prétentions. Dans sa décision, le tribunal a estimé que « les éléments constitutifs du délit d’outrage prévu par l’article 658 du Code pénal ne sont pas réunis à la charge des prévenus », et qu’il en était de même pour les faits de violences ou de voies de fait prévus par l’article 240 du Code pénal. La juge Fanta Alama Camara, qui présidait l’audience, a notamment relevé qu’« aucun acte matériel constitutif d’outrage ou de violence ou encore de voies de fait n’est établi ni personnellement imputable » aux prévenus. En conséquence, le tribunal a prononcé leur relaxe et débouté le ministère public de ses réquisitions. Sur l’action civile, la juridiction a également rejeté la demande de la partie civile qui réclamait le paiement de 100 millions de francs guinéens à titre de dommages et intérêts. Elle a aussi rejeté la demande de comparution des prévenus, faute d’éléments suffisants. Les dépens ont été mis à la charge de la partie civile. Cette décision met ainsi fin, en première instance, à la procédure engagée contre les trois responsables syndicaux de la BCRG. Elisa CAMARA L’article TPI de Kaloum : les trois leaders syndicaux de la BCRG renvoyés des fins de la poursuite est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .
